TILE EMISSION vs THE OBJECT BONFIRE — root cause, for when you have time. The maintainer has chased this ~6 times over months. It is not a tuning problem and it is not the art; the two fires go through two DIFFERENT systems and only one of them is a light. OBJECT bonfire (WorldScene.ts:4820): sl.push({col,row,z, radius:7, color:[1.9,0.88,0.3], flicker:1}) — a real ShaderLight in the fragment loop, radius in CELLS, colour OVERBRIGHT (>1 widens the hot plateau since the multiplier clamps at 1.25), with att=(1-dist/radius)^2, LOS shadows and elevation. TILE bonfire (WorldScene.ts:7270): propStamps.push({radius: (em.radius+0.5)*sqrt2*dx ~113px, alpha: min(0.85, avgS*0.7) ~0.53}) — an additive stamp painted into the glow RenderTexture OVER the already-darkened frame. Additive overlay cannot un-darken the night grade; it can only add colour on top, capped at 0.85. THE KICKER: the real path was built and never wired. ShaderLight declares 'radius: in cells; NEGATIVE = shadow-free GLOW pool (tile emission)' and the shader implements it ('Sign of w: positive = a real light; NEGATIVE = a GLOW pool from tile emission', nightlight.ts:555). But there are exactly THREE sl.push sites in the whole client — debug probe, campfire radius 7, torches radius 6 — and ZERO negative radii anywhere. So tile emission never reaches a light slot. Your comment at 4822 says why: 'emission glow pools live in the additive glow field, not in light slots — they can't be crowded out', i.e. a deliberate trade to stop emissive tiles eating the 12 MAX_SHADER_LIGHTS. The cost is that they emit no light at all. WHAT WOULD CLOSE IT: (1) push emissive props into sl with a NEGATIVE radius — the prop loop at 7250 already has p.col/p.row/lvl, exactly the grid coords ShaderLight wants; (2) budget the slots — reserve 2-4, rank by distance x strength, so torches cannot starve them (the original worry, now solvable rather than avoided); (3) per-TILE radius/intensity — rCells comes from em.radius which is per-MATERIAL, so a bonfire and a glowing mushroom on grass get identical light size; the schema models 'this material glows', not 'this tile contains a fire'; (4) an overbright gain — 0..1 source colours cannot make a hot plateau the way [1.9,0.88,0.3] does. On my side I just fixed the art half: the harmonizer had been recolouring the flame's hot core to grass-teal, so the tile's own glow colour was being sampled from the dim rim. Its main source is now r=6.9 s=0.79 warm orange [0.93,0.60,0.17] (was r=2.8 s=0.56 dark blood-red). Better halo — but a halo is all the tile path can currently produce.
